# Block 1: AI-assisted R programming {.unnumbered} ## Prerequisites - A GitHub account, an IDE (RStudio or Positron), and experience with Git, `renv` and `testthat` from earlier days. - **Claude Code**, the workshop's main tool, installed and checked before the day: follow [Setting up Claude Code](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd), which also lists the accounts it works with. - **An Anthropic API key** for [Block 6](11k-build-an-agent.qmd), where you build your own agent in R. It is separate from a Claude subscription; [Setting up Claude Code](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd#api-key) shows how to get one and test it. - **Posit Assistant** works as an alternative for most blocks; each block has a collapsed *Using another tool* callout saying where it differs. - Your institution's permission to use these tools, and, near research data, your ethics approval and data agreements. Block 3 covers this. GitHub Copilot is needed only for the two self-study pages: [inline completions](11b-inline-completions.qmd) (Copilot Free is enough) and the [Copilot cloud agent](11l-copilot-cloud-agent.qmd) (a plan that includes it). ## Learning outcomes By the end of the day you will be able to: 1. Explain what a large language model is, how a tool differs from the model behind it, and why what is in its context window matters (this block). 2. Debug your own code with AI, and know when AI helps most ([Block 2: Debugging with AI](11c-debugging.qmd)). 3. Choose how much an agent may do, and know every route by which your data leave your machine ([Block 3: Context, disclosure and autonomy](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd)). 4. Write an `AGENTS.md` instruction fileA file the assistant loads into every conversation, such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, stating the project’s standing conventions. Its contents are requests, not guarantees., install a skillA reusable procedure for one kind of task: a folder containing a SKILL.md file (and optionally scripts and templates) that an assistant loads only when it is invoked by name or judged relevant from its description., and test that they load ([Block 4: Instructions and skills](11e-instructions-skills.qmd)). 5. Protect files with a permission rule, and detect any change with git ([Block 5: Enforced controls](11f-enforced-controls.qmd)). 6. Build a small agent in R, and say where approvals and permission rules act inside it ([Block 6: Build your own agent in R](11k-build-an-agent.qmd)). 7. Have an agent clean data against a codebook you own, and check it with tests and validation ([Block 7: Data cleaning and validation](11g-data-cleaning.qmd)). 8. Have an agent refactor code under a characterisation testA test that checks new code reproduces the saved output of the original code exactly. It shows the output is unchanged, not that it is correct., with the reference in your hands ([Block 8: Functionalise a script step](11i-characterisation-tests.qmd)). 9. Use AI as a code reviewer, and grade it against the Day 2 answer key ([Block 9: AI-assisted code review](11h-code-review.qmd)). ## Materials You work in your own copy of a workshop template repository. You fork it before the day and use it in every block from Block 2 to Block 8, and on the self-study page on the Copilot cloud agent ([its layout, and what each block uses](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd#your-workshop-repository)). Block 9 works in a separate folder, `~/ai-review`, so that the AI reviewer sees only the script under review. Every block ends with a *Going further* section that is not covered live. The two self-study pages listed under *Prerequisites* are for after the day. **Verification is the workshop's only non-negotiable.** It lets you automate with confidence. Once you can check an agent's work quickly and independently, you can hand it more of the work. Every exercise ends with that check. ## The thread through the day: Check · Reproduce · Record Every block applies three habits, and ends with a box saying what it added: - **Check.** Treat what an AI produces as a claim. Verify it independently against the data, a test, a reference you hold, the Git pane's diff (Positron: the Source Control view), or your own knowledge of the biology. - **Reproduce.** The code runs in a fresh R sessionAn R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with “never save .RData” set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record. with the package versions in the lockfileThe renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment., and nothing changed that you did not see. - **Record.** Leave the evidence a reader needs: a codebookA table describing each variable: its type, valid range, missing-value codes, unit and label mappings. It is the data dictionary from Day 2 with machine-readable rules, and you own it, not the AI., logs of every data change, numbers computed in code, and an AI-use logA record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README.. ::::::: {.dia .dia-flow role="figure" aria-label="Files that accumulate in your workshop repository through the day, block by block: Block 3 adds docs/ai-log.md, your AI-use log; Block 4 adds your edits to AGENTS.md, and a skill; Block 5 adds a permission rule to .claude/settings.json and tests it; Block 6 adds summaries.R, written by your own agent; Block 7 adds the codebook, and the cleaning and exclusion logs; Block 8 adds the reference and tests."} ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} **Block 3** `docs/ai-log.md`, your AI-use log ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} **Block 4** edits to `AGENTS.md`, and a skill ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} **Block 5** a permission rule in `.claude/settings.json`, and its test ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} **Block 6** `summaries.R`, written by your own agent ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} **Block 7** the codebook, and the cleaning and exclusion logs ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} **Block 8** reference and tests ::: ::: {.dia-caption} What your repository holds by the end of the day, block by block. ::: ::::::: **Your AI-use log.** From Block 3, after each block in which an agent does work, you add one line to `docs/ai-log.md`. The agent can draft it, but the last part, what you kept or changed, is yours to write. It is the record a journal or funder asks for when you declare AI use. Each line has this form: ```text date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed ``` ## Claude Code quick reference {#cc-quick-reference} Keep this open during the day. Type each command at the Claude Code prompt, unless the row says otherwise ([where am I typing?](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd#where-am-i-typing)). ### Start, stop and leave | To... | Do this | |-------|-------------| | Start Claude Code in your workshop repository | Open the project in RStudio or Positron, then type `claude` in its Terminal tab | | Stop it while it is working | Esc, or `Ctrl+C` once (when nothing is running, a second `Ctrl+C` exits Claude Code) | | Start a new conversation, with nothing from the last one | `/clear` | | Run one shell command without leaving Claude Code | Start the line with `!`. The output is added to the conversation, so it reaches the model | | Leave | `/exit` | ### Approvals and modes | To... | Do this | |-------|-------------| | Ask for a plan before anything changes | `/plan` followed by your request, for example `/plan add a mass_change_g column` | | Answer a request to edit a file or run a command | Plain **Yes** or **No**. Never choose an option that says *don't ask again*: it saves a rule that skips the question from then on | | Approve a plan it made in plan mode, and still approve each edit | **Yes, manually approve edits**. It is not the first option: the first (*Yes, and use auto mode*, or *Yes, auto-accept edits*) switches approvals off | | Change a plan before you approve it | **No, keep planning**, then say what to change | | Approve a plan a skill shows you | Reply in the chat, for example *Yes, go ahead*, or say what to change | | Change how much it may do without asking | `Shift+Tab` cycles the modes: Manual (`default`) → `acceptEdits` → `plan`, and `auto` where available | | See or add permission rules | `/permissions` | ### Models and effort | To... | Do this | |-------|-------------| | See which model and effort level you are using, for your AI-use log | Both are shown at the top of the session | | Choose a model from a list | `/model`, then the arrow keys. **Enter** switches and saves it as your default for new sessions; **s** switches for this session only | | Switch model straight away | `/model sonnet`, `/model opus` or `/model haiku`. This also saves it as your default | | Change how much it thinks before answering (the effort level) | `/effort` opens a slider; `/effort high` sets a level directly (`low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` or `max`); `/effort auto` goes back to the model's default | The defaults are fine for today. A larger model or a higher effort level is slower and uses more tokensThe unit a model reads and writes, roughly three-quarters of an English word. Providers charge per token, and because the whole conversation is re-sent with each request, a long conversation costs more per question.. ### Instructions and skills | To... | Do this | |-------|-------------| | Check your instruction file is loaded | `/memory` should list `AGENTS.md`; edit the file itself from the Files pane | | List the skills it can use | `/skills` | | Start an instruction file for a project of your own | Ask Claude to assess the project and draft an `AGENTS.md` in its reply, then prune it; or `/init`, which writes a `CLAUDE.md` that describes the project | **Never run `/init` in the workshop repository**, or in any project that has an `AGENTS.md`. Once a `CLAUDE.md` or `CLAUDE.local.md` exists, Claude Code stops reading `AGENTS.md` ([Block 4: Instructions and skills](11e-instructions-skills.qmd)). ### Checking, privacy and working away from your desk | To... | Do this | |-------|-------------| | Check its work while it runs | Use the R console and the Git pane, not the Terminal tab Claude Code is using: see [checking work](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd#checking-work) | | Check your privacy settings (Pro and Max accounts) | `/privacy-settings` | | Carry on this session from your phone or a browser (Remote Control) | `/remote-control` (or `/rc`) links the session to claude.ai/code or the Claude mobile app. Type it again to disconnect | Remote Control is not needed on the day. It needs a Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise login; it does not work with an API key, and on Team and Enterprise plans an Owner must switch it on first. Claude Code keeps running on your computer, with the same files, permission rules and approvals, so the computer and the `claude` process must stay on. An approval you tap on your phone follows the same rule as one at your desk. Your workshop repository starts Claude Code in **Manual** mode (`default`): it asks before every edit and before most commands (read-only ones, such as `head`, run without asking). Claude Code's own default is `auto`, where a second model approves actions for you; [Block 3: Context, disclosure and autonomy](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd) explains the difference. Stay in Manual and read each request before you answer. **One rule for every approval:** approve a run only if you can say what it does and why you want it now; refusing is always safe. ## Framing: tools, models and context This block introduces the two words you will use all day, the three tools and how they differ, what a large language model is, and why its context window matters. *⏱ ~20 minutes: presentation, a short discussion and a quiz, while any set-up problems are sorted out.* ### Assistants and agents Two words recur all day. An assistantAny AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course “assistant” is the general word; “agent” is used when the tool acts on your files. is any AI tool that helps you write or understand code. An agentAn assistant that can read across a project’s files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises. is an assistant that acts: it reads your project and, if you let it, edits files and runs commands. Claude Code and Posit Assistant are agents; a chat window that only answers is not. To see how one works inside, you build a small one yourself in [Block 6: Build your own agent in R](11k-build-an-agent.qmd). ### Three tools, and the models behind them The course uses three tools. They differ in where you type, what they can read and what they may do. GitHub Copilot appears twice: in the editor, and as a cloud agent on GitHub. ::::::: {.dia .dia-lanes role="figure" aria-label="Where you type in each tool, what it reads and what it may do. Claude Code, the main tool all day: you type in the Terminal tab; it reads your project folder and the output of its own commands, but not your R console; it may edit files and run commands, asking first in Manual mode. Posit Assistant, the alternative in most blocks: you type in its chat pane in RStudio or Positron; it reads project files and your live R session, including the names and types of your objects; it may edit files and run R code in your session, as its mode allows. GitHub Copilot in the editor, self-study: you type code in a script; it reads your open files; it offers grey suggestions you accept with Tab or ignore. Claude is a family of models: Claude Code is one tool that uses them, and Posit Assistant and Copilot can use Claude models too. ::: ::::::: | Tool | Where you use it | Models it can use | In this course | |---|---|---|---| | Claude Code | The Terminal tab of RStudio or Positron | Anthropic's Claude models | The main tool, in every block from Block 2 | | Posit Assistant | A chat pane inside RStudio or Positron | Models through Posit AI Pass, or your own provider key (for example, Claude models with an Anthropic API key) | The alternative in most blocks: see each block's *Using another tool* callout | | GitHub Copilot | Inline suggestions in the editor; the cloud agent on github.com | A choice of models, including Claude, GPT and Gemini | The two self-study pages only | You do not need strong opinions about which model is best. You only need to know that the choice exists and changes the output. ### What is a large language model? A large language model (LLM) predicts the next fragment of text from what came before. It has learnt from a large share of the public internet, code included. Every tool today is built on one. Models differ in code quality and in how often they invent functions that do not exist. If a model gives you consistently poor suggestions and your plan lets you switch, try another: switching is a cheap experiment. **Model and effort level.** Two settings change what you get. The **model** is which LLM answers: larger models, such as Opus, are more capable and cost more per token; smaller ones, such as Sonnet and Haiku, are faster and cheaper. The effort levelHow much a model reasons before it answers. In Claude Code it runs from low to max; a higher level can help with hard problems, but it is slower and uses more tokens. sets how much the model thinks before it answers: higher effort can help with hard problems, but it is slower and uses more tokens. The [quick reference](#cc-quick-reference) shows how to change both. Whatever you use, record the model in your AI-use log. ### Why the context window matters An LLM has no memory between calls: each one starts with only what you supply, up to the limit of its context windowThe maximum amount of text a language model can consider in one call. The model has no memory between calls, so it sees only what is in the context window.. That one fact explains the day. Instruction files and skills give the model context it would not otherwise have. They are only requests, so Block 5 adds controls that hold whether or not the model follows them, and tests check the result. **Remember:** the model sees only what reaches its context window, and everything that reaches it has left your machine. ### Discussion Take three minutes, then post a short answer to each question in the Zoom chat: 1. What is one task you would like to hand to an agent by the end of the day, and how would you check it? Is there anything you would not delegate at all? 2. How do you use AI tools now: browser chat, IDE chat, a terminal agent? ### Check your understanding **Your instruction file asks the agent never to edit `data/raw/`. Why does the course still add permission rules and tests?**
**True or false: a large language model has no memory between calls, so each interaction starts with only the context you supply.** **True or false: Claude models can be used only through Claude Code.** ## Going further (not covered live) This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you. :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Changing the model in other tools In Posit Assistant, use its model picker. In Copilot Chat, use the model menu (inline completions have a separate setting). In R, `ellmer::chat_anthropic()` takes the model as `model =`, and the effort level as `params = params(reasoning_effort = "low")`; [Block 6](11k-build-an-agent.qmd) sets the model this way. ::: :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Two modes of execution The tools you use today are **synchronous and local**: they act on files on your machine, respond in seconds, and can be interrupted. An **asynchronous, remote** agent, such as the Copilot cloud agent, works on its own branch on someone else's servers. It returns a pull request minutes later; the self-study page on the [Copilot cloud agent](11l-copilot-cloud-agent.qmd) walks through it. The first kind invites you to watch and interrupt. The second invites you to write a precise specification and review what comes back. Block 3 turns this into a ladder of autonomy. ::: :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## The thread, in more detail Day 1 introduced `renv`; Day 4 checks that an agent has kept to it. On Day 2 you saw what a reviewable project needs ([TADA! and the README](06-reproducibility.qmd#repro-fix), and [the SORTEE checklist](06-reproducibility.qmd#repro-sortee)). Day 4 shows how AI can help produce that record without inventing any of it. Many journals, funders and institutions now ask authors to declare AI use, and a log written at the time is easier and more accurate than one reconstructed later. ::: ## Glossary ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
term definition
agent An assistant that can read across a project's files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises.
AI-use log A record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README.
assistant Any AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course "assistant" is the general word; "agent" is used when the tool acts on your files.
characterisation test A test that checks new code reproduces the saved output of the original code exactly. It shows the output is unchanged, not that it is correct.
codebook A table describing each variable: its type, valid range, missing-value codes, unit and label mappings. It is the data dictionary from Day 2 with machine-readable rules, and you own it, not the AI.
context window The maximum amount of text a language model can consider in one call. The model has no memory between calls, so it sees only what is in the context window.
effort level How much a model reasons before it answers. In Claude Code it runs from low to max; a higher level can help with hard problems, but it is slower and uses more tokens.
fresh R session An R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with "never save .RData" set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record.
instruction file A file the assistant loads into every conversation, such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, stating the project's standing conventions. Its contents are requests, not guarantees.
large language model A model trained on a large body of text, code included, that predicts the next fragment of text from what came before. Claude, GPT and Gemini are families of large language models; tools such as Claude Code, Posit Assistant and GitHub Copilot send your requests to one.
lockfile The renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment.
skill A reusable procedure for one kind of task: a folder containing a SKILL.md file (and optionally scripts and templates) that an assistant loads only when it is invoked by name or judged relevant from its description.
token The unit a model reads and writes, roughly three-quarters of an English word. Providers charge per token, and because the whole conversation is re-sent with each request, a long conversation costs more per question.
````` ::: :::
